topStories.headline: SoMa's Police Station Loses Its Fourth Captain Since Last June
topStories.dek: Captain Carla Hurley is stepping down from Southern Station, leaving the district that covers SoMa, Mission Bay, Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island without stable leadership for the fourth time in eighteen months.
topStories.body:
Captain Carla Hurley, who has led Southern Station since May 2026, announced in a Tuesday email to city leaders and community members that she will leave her post this Saturday. The departure marks the fourth captain change at the station since June 2025, a churn of leadership that neighborhood advocates say is deepening a crisis of accountability and response in one of the city's highest-crime districts.

Southern Station's jurisdiction covers a broad swath of the eastern city — SoMa, the Embarcadero, Market Street, China Basin, Mission Bay, Yerba Buena Island and Treasure Island. In a November 3 email to constituents, Hurley acknowledged the station's long-standing struggles with response times and staffing shortages, noting those problems predate her tenure.

Shaun Aukland, a SoMa resident and member of the SoMa West Neighborhood Association, told Mission Local that the ongoing leadership churn is damaging the district's ability to build community trust. "The Police District with the highest crime rate continues to churn through leadership, unfortunately, and lacks stability," Aukland wrote.

Hurley's replacement, the incoming captain, was named as a defendant in a 2026 lawsuit by the parents of Jon-Marques Psalms, a 30-year-old man who died in 2025 as a result of police training exercises. The department has not publicly commented on the transition timeline or on the lawsuit.

topStories.headline: Airbnb's Brian Chesky Gives $100 Million to SF Parks — Potrero Hill's Jackson Playground Among First Beneficiaries
topStories.dek: San Francisco's largest single-donor parks gift ever will direct $39 million in phase one funding to five projects, including a full renovation of Potrero Hill's Jackson Playground.
topStories.body:
Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky announced on November 11 that he will donate $100 million to San Francisco parks — the largest single-donor gift the city has ever received for parks — with Mayor Daniel Lurie calling on other philanthropists to follow his lead. The gift will be delivered in two phases.

The first phase allocates $39 million to five projects spread across SoMa, the Mission, Bayview-Hunters Point, Potrero Hill and the downtown waterfront. For residents in these neighborhoods, the most direct impact will be a full renovation of Potrero Hill's Jackson Playground, which is slated to receive funding through this initial tranche.

The Potrero Hill investment is one of several neighborhood-level improvements funded in phase one. The gift will also pay for expanded pool hours at Garfield Square in the Mission, help close a construction funding gap at India Basin Waterfront Park in Bayview-Hunters Point, and fund a plan to merge Embarcadero Plaza and Sue Bierman Park into a single five-acre waterfront park.

Chesky grew up in the Bay Area and has spoken publicly about his attachment to San Francisco. No completion timeline for the Jackson Playground renovation was announced, though the city confirmed the phase-one projects at the time of the gift's announcement.

topStories.headline: Dogpatch Power Station Developer Threw a Party Around a Mysterious Tiny Waterfront Building
topStories.dek: Fifth Space, the developer behind the 29-acre Dogpatch Power Station project, held a public competition for ideas on what to do with a small completed structure on the site — drawing neighbors curious about the multibillion-dollar project's direction.
topStories.body:
A small building that appeared on San Francisco's central waterfront without explanation generated enough neighborhood buzz that Fifth Space, the development company behind the Dogpatch Power Station project, held an open competition for ideas about its use, inviting those with the best proposals to tour the property. The story was reported by the San Francisco Chronicle on November 6, 2026.

"The community was asking, 'What is this thing?'" said Enrique Landa, CEO of Fifth Space. "People in the community were calling us up. They had questions."

The Dogpatch Power Station development is a 29-acre, multibillion-dollar project that the city's Board of Supervisors approved by a unanimous vote in 2020. At buildout, the project envisions thousands of housing units — 30 percent of them below market rate — alongside offices, retail, and a 250-room hotel, plus possible medical space tied to UCSF's nearby Mission Bay campus. So far, one building has been completed: a 105-unit workforce housing complex named after former Supervisor Sophie Maxwell, who led the fight to close the coal-burning power plant that once occupied the site.

Among the competition entries: a Dogpatch resident of 16 years proposed the building house an influencer who could not leave until the UCSF building is finished; an attorney suggested it become a "Taco Bell for the 1%." Fifth Space has not publicly announced what the structure will ultimately be used for.

moreNews.headline: SF Board of Supervisors Unanimously Legalizes Home-Kitchen Food Businesses
moreNews.body: On Tuesday, November 11, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to approve an ordinance allowing street vendors to prepare and sell food cooked in their own homes, bringing the city in line with a state program called Microenterprise Home Kitchen Operations (MEHKO) that has been running in many Bay Area counties for years. Under the new rules, the city's Department of Public Health will create a permitting and inspection program for home kitchens; an annual permit will cost $828, far less than the $1,000-or-more monthly fees vendors have faced renting commercial commissary kitchens. The legislation was introduced by Supervisor Jackie Fielder after vendors protested an earlier ordinance that required more expensive equipment and commercial kitchen access.

moreNews.headline: Treasure Island Density Proposal Would Push Housing Count to 10,800 Units
moreNews.body: A revised development proposal for Treasure Island, reported by the San Francisco Chronicle in January 2026 and still moving through city review, would increase the number of planned housing units on the island by up to 35 percent — from 8,000 homes to as many as 10,800. The amendment aims to build on momentum from the past five years, during which about 1,000 units have been completed alongside eight new waterfront parks and a ferry terminal offering 10-minute connections to downtown. Phase one of the broader redevelopment was marked in July 2026 by the opening of 490 Avenue of the Palms, a six-story, 148-unit condominium building — the first condo complex completed on the island.

moreNews.headline: SFMTA Moving Forward on Paid Parking for Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island
moreNews.body: The SFMTA Board of Directors voted on March 3, 2026 to approve a proposal for on-street metered parking on Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island. The agency, working in partnership with the Treasure Island Development Authority, is now preparing an implementation plan. The move is part of a broader transportation strategy for the islands as the resident population grows with ongoing construction.
